messages.content: Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers suits variable, high-frequency work. A producer pushes jobs onto a queue (SQS, Redis, RabbitMQ) and a pool of workers pulls them off as capacity allows. This gives near-real-time processing, natural retries via dead-letter queues, and horizontal scaling — add workers and throughput rises. You manage broker infrastructure, handle idempotency for retried jobs, and watch for backlog growth if workers fall behind producers.

Scheduled batch runs suit predictable, periodic work — nightly reports, data syncs, cleanup tasks. A cron trigger fires a job on a fixed interval, processes a bounded chunk of data, then exits. No broker, no long-running worker fleet, and failures show up as a single run rather than scattered across a queue. Work waits for the next scheduled slot, and batches can grow unwieldy if data volume spikes between runs.

Most teams end up running both: a queue for user-triggered, latency-sensitive events, and batch jobs for aggregate or maintenance work where a few minutes' delay is fine. Choose a queue if jobs are bursty and need fast turnaround. Choose a scheduled batch if work is inherently periodic and volume is predictable — it's simpler to build and cheaper to run.
